native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: Educational attainment rises far more steeply with family socioeconomic status for Black respondents than for non-Black non-Hispanic respondents in this NLSY79 cohort, so the Black attainment shortfall is concentrated entirely at low SES and disappears at higher SES: below the pooled SES median Black respondents completed grade 12 or more at 53.5% vs 74.1% for non-Black non-Hispanic respondents (gap -20.7 pp, 95% CI -27.0 to -14.4; RR 0.72), while at or above the median the groups are statistically indistinguishable (89.2% vs 90.2%; gap -1.0 pp, 95% CI -6.3 to +4.2; RR 0.99), a race-by-SES interaction confirmed by LR tests (Black-only chi2 = 7.01, df 1, p = 0.008; interaction OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.19-4.06). The Black SES gradient is +35.7 pp (53.5 to 89.2) versus +16.1 pp (74.1 to 90.2) for the comparison group, so high family background buys Black students about twice as much additional schooling but never lifts them above their socioeconomic peers - no SES stratum, including the descriptive grade>=16 appendix (Black 0.25% vs 0.38%, Fisher p = 0.52), shows a Black advantage - and true BA completion is unobserved in this extract (only 37 respondents at grade >= 16, 5 of them Black, measured when respondents were 14-22), so the finding is an association about SES-conditioned attainment gradients, not a causal or institutional claim.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61), cleaned sentinels (grade 95 -> missing, wealth -250 -> missing) and handled top-coded money variables via rank-based cuts. 2) Built outcome ladder: P3 primary = grade >= 12 among respondents aged >= 20 in 1979 (n=3,487); P1 = grade >= 13; P2 = ever DORM/FRATERNITY/SORORITY residence 1981-96; descriptive appendix = grade >= 16 with Wilson and exact CIs. 3) Built background SES index (z of max parental grade, z of occupation major-group prestige rank validated against parental education and 1979 income, z of log family income 1979; >= 2 of 3 items; 11,747 respondents). 4) Applied the pre-registered granularity rule: tertiles failed the n>=100 cell test (Black 257/108/86) so levels collapsed to below/at-or-above pooled median (smallest cell 148, none < 50); tertile results retained as flagged descriptive. 5) Stratified rate tables with Wilson CIs, percentage-point gaps and rate ratios (Black and Hispanic vs non-Black non-Hispanic reference). 6) Logistic models with age (linear+quadratic) and sex, BLACK x SES interaction and LR tests, plus model-predicted gaps. 7) Robustness: occupation prestige coding vs continuous -code, complete-case, occupation dropped, single-proxy indices, endogenous 1985-1996 wealth/income/savings direction checks, missing-indicator diagnostic; no outcome imputation. 8) ASVAB mean-Z attenuation check on a common subsample (reported as attenuation, not mediation). 9) Wrote tables, model summaries and RESULTS_summary.md under outputs/.

sub_hypo.text: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower socioeconomic status levels, with a coefficient of 0.7606 for the interaction between socioeconomic status and being Black.
sub_hypo.context: Students in the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY79), comparing the Black-student advantage across socioeconomic status levels.
variables: BA degree completion (no explicit column specified)
sub_hypo.relations: Socioeconomic status moderates the association between being Black and BA degree completion: the advantage for Black students is greater at lower socioeconomic status levels. The socioeconomic status × being Black interaction coefficient is 0.7606.
